questions.q: What does the chapter call the process of taking decisions, organising the society's life with different sets of rules, and ensuring that the rules are followed?
questions.a: Governance

questions.q: On a busy railway platform in Nagpur, about 2,000 passengers wait for their trains at the same time. Going by the chapter, why does such a place need rules?
questions.a: When a large number of people are together there can be disagreements and disorder, and rules keep order and harmony.
o: Many people together can lead to disorder; rules keep order and harmony
Rules are needed only so that a court can punish the guilty people
Rules are needed only at places where employers and employees work
Rules are needed only once a law has been passed by the legislature

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Rules and laws are not set once and for all.
Reason (R): Citizens also have a say in the laws and rules governing the society, just as a student body might ask a school to change a rule.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: because citizens have a say in the rules, the rules can be discussed and changed.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: True or False? 'At a workplace, rules bind the employer as well as the employees.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. People employed in jobs follow the rules set by their employer, and the employer must also follow the rules which it has committed to its employees.
s: States the verdict: True
Reason: employees follow the employer's rules, and the employer must follow the rules it committed to its employees

questions.q: (a) Define 'government' as the chapter does. (b) What are some of the more important rules made by a government called?
questions.a: (a) The group of individuals or the system that makes the rules and ensures that they are followed is called a government. (b) Laws.
s: (a) The group of individuals or the system that makes the rules and ensures they are followed
(b) Laws

questions.q:
The town library in Shimla has two rules: a book must be returned within 14 days, and readers must keep silent in the reading hall. A library committee decides the rules and the librarian makes sure readers follow them.
(a) Which part of this matches the chapter's meaning of 'governance'?
(b) A group of college readers asks the committee to keep the reading hall open until 8 pm. Which idea from the chapter does their request show?
questions.a: (a) Governance is the whole process of taking decisions, organising life with rules and ensuring they are followed: here the committee deciding the rules and the librarian seeing that they are followed. (b) Rules are not set once and for all; the people who follow them have a say in changing them, just as a student body might ask the school or university management to change a rule.
s: (a) Identifies deciding the rules and making sure they are followed (committee plus librarian) as governance
(b) Rules are not fixed for ever; those governed can ask for a rule to be changed

questions.q:
Answer briefly from the chapter.
(i) Name the two groups in a school who, the chapter says, each have rules to follow.
(ii) What does the chapter say would happen if no one followed the rules?
(iii) Why do rules become necessary when a large number of people live together?
questions.a: (i) Students and teachers. (ii) Society would not be able to function. (iii) When many people live together there can be disagreements and disorder, so rules are needed to maintain order and harmony.
s: (i) Students and teachers
(ii) Society would not be able to function
(iii) Many people together cause disagreements and disorder; rules keep order and harmony

questions.q: Sameer says: 'Governance and government are just two names for the same thing.' How far is he right? Explain using the chapter's meaning of each word.
questions.a: He is only partly right. The two are closely linked, because a government is what carries out governance. But they are not the same: governance is a process (taking decisions, organising the society's life with rules and ensuring they are followed), while a government is the group of individuals or the system that makes the rules and ensures they are followed.
s: States the meaning of governance as a process of deciding, organising with rules and ensuring they are followed
States the meaning of government as the group or system that makes and enforces the rules
Verdict: partly right; linked, but one is the process and the other the body that does it

questions.q:
A 10-day sports camp in Ranchi housed 240 students from 8 schools in one hostel. For the first 2 days there were no camp rules, and the organisers received 18 complaints about pushing in the meal queue, lights left on late and missing kit. On day 3 the organisers met, made 5 rules (such as queuing school by school and lights out at 9:30 pm) and appointed 8 senior students to see that they were followed. Over the remaining 8 days only 6 complaints came in. On day 6 the 8 school captains together asked the organisers to move lights out to 10 pm on the two nights of evening matches.
(a) What does the chapter call what the organisers began on day 3?
(b) Find the average number of complaints per day before the rules and after them.
(c) Using the chapter, explain why the first two days produced so many complaints.
(d) Should the organisers agree to the captains' request? Give your judgement, using the chapter's idea about rules and the camp's data.
questions.a: (a) Governance: taking decisions, organising life with rules and ensuring the rules are followed. (b) Before: 18 / 2 = 9 complaints a day; after: 6 / 8 = 0.75 a day. (c) A large number of people were living together with no rules, which led to disagreements and disorder. (d) The request deserves a hearing, because rules are not set once and for all and the people governed by them may ask for a change, as a student body may ask its school. But the data show the rules cut complaints from 9 to 0.75 a day, so the organisers should change the rule only in a limited way (for example only on the two match nights, as asked) and keep watch that disorder does not return.
s: (a) Governance
(b) 9 complaints a day before; 0.75 a day after
(c) Many people living together without rules leads to disagreements and disorder
(d) A justified judgement weighing the right to ask for a rule change against the drop in complaints the rules brought

questions.q:
Anjali, a Class 6 student in Guwahati, notices rules all through one day. Answer each part from the chapter.
(a) Students at her school must stand in line at assembly. Which other group at the school also has rules of its own, according to the chapter?
(b) Her elder brother is appearing for his board examinations. What does the chapter say such students must do?
(c) Her father stops the car at a red signal on the way to school. Which kind of rules is he obeying?
(d) Her mother's company gives every worker the weekly holiday it promised when they joined. Whose duty under the rules does this show?
(e) Suppose her State makes a rule, binding on everyone, that no one may use a mobile phone while driving. What does the chapter call such an important rule made by a government?
questions.a: (a) The teachers. (b) Students appearing for examinations must follow certain rules. (c) Traffic rules. (d) The employer's: employers must also follow the rules they have committed to their employees. (e) A law.
s: (a) Teachers
(b) Follow certain rules for the examination
(c) Traffic rules
(d) The employer must follow the rules it committed to its employees
(e) A law

questions.q: Which organ of government implements, or 'executes', the laws?
questions.a: The executive

questions.q: A court in Bhubaneswar hears the case of a man accused of cheating people through fake shopping websites. It finds him guilty and sentences him to a fine and three years in jail. Which organ of government is at work here?
questions.a: The judiciary, the system of courts that decides whether someone has broken the law and what action, including punishment, should follow.

questions.q:
Match each item in Column A with its description in Column B.
Column A:
1. Legislature
2. Executive
3. Judiciary
4. Separation of powers
Column B:
A. Implements the laws
B. Decides whether someone has broken a law and what action should follow
C. Keeping the three organs separate so that each can check the others
D. Makes new laws and sometimes updates or removes existing ones

Consider the following statements about the organs of government.
I. The separation of powers is intended to provide a system of checks and balances.
II. Under the separation of powers, the legislature, the executive and the judiciary do not interact with each other at all.
III. The judiciary sometimes examines whether a law passed by the legislature is well conceived and fair to all.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: the three organs are kept separate, but they interact with each other and work together.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Many governments have passed new laws to fight cybercrime.
Reason (R): Till about 30 years ago, people in India sent money to a distant relative by queuing at the Post Office for a money order.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. The new laws came because digital ways of sending money created a new class of criminals who steal money digitally; the old money order system does not explain them.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: True or False? 'The executive is the organ of government that makes new laws.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The legislature makes new laws (it 'legislates'); the executive implements, or 'executes', the laws.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: the legislature makes laws; the executive implements them

questions.q: What is meant by the 'separation of powers'? What is it intended to provide?
questions.a: The separation of powers means that the three organs of government (legislature, executive and judiciary) are kept separate, although they interact with each other and work together. It is intended to provide a system of checks and balances: each organ can check what the other is doing and restore balance if one acts beyond its expected role.
s: The three organs are kept separate though they interact and work together
It provides checks and balances: each organ can check the others and restore balance

questions.q:
Farmers in a State complain that some shops are selling fake seeds. Three things then happen.
(i) The State Assembly passes a law making the sale of fake seeds a crime.
(ii) The police raid a shop in Warangal and seize 300 packets of fake seeds.
(iii) A court finds the shop owner guilty and fines him.
For each step, name the organ of government at work and the job the chapter gives that organ.
questions.a: (i) The legislature, which makes new laws through an assembly of representatives of the people. (ii) The executive, which implements the laws; the police are the agency responsible for enforcing law and order. (iii) The judiciary, the system of courts that decides whether someone has broken the law and what action, including punishment, should follow.
s: (i) Legislature: makes the law
(ii) Executive: implements and enforces the law through the police
(iii) Judiciary: decides that the law was broken and the punishment

questions.q:
Use the chapter's example of cybercrime to answer these four parts.
(a) What change in the way people send money gave rise to a new class of criminals?
(b) What did many governments do about it?
(c) Which agency of the executive deals with such criminals in the chapter's example?
(d) What usually happens to such criminals once they are convicted in court?
questions.a: (a) Money orders and demand drafts gave way to digital means of sending money instantly, and some criminals found digital ways of stealing people's money without leaving their desks. (b) They passed new laws to fight such criminal activities (cybercrime); this is the legislature's work. (c) The cyber police. (d) They are usually fined as well as jailed for some years.
s: (a) Digital means of sending money let criminals steal money digitally
(b) Governments passed new laws against cybercrime
(c) The cyber police
(d) Usually fined and jailed for some years

questions.q:
Read this imaginary account from the State of Sundarpradesh.
Step 1: The State Assembly passes a law that every building of more than four floors must have a fire exit.
Step 2: The State's housing minister then orders that buildings owned by his friends need not follow this law.
Step 3: A resident takes the matter to court. The court examines the minister's order and cancels it.
Step 4: The police then check all such buildings and fine the owners who have no fire exit.
(a) Which organ of government acted in Step 1, and which in Step 4?
(b) Which organ acted in Step 3, and which of its jobs did it perform?
(c) Which organ acted beyond its expected role in Step 2? Explain why.
(d) How does this account show the system of checks and balances at work?
(e) What might have happened to the residents if the minister had also controlled the court?
questions.a: (a) Step 1: the legislature (it made the law); Step 4: the executive (the police enforce the law). (b) The judiciary; it examined whether a decision taken by the executive was right. (c) The executive (the minister is part of it): its job is to implement the law, but he tried to set it aside for some people, going beyond its expected role. (d) One organ, the judiciary, checked what another, the executive, was doing and restored balance by cancelling the order, after which the law was enforced for all. (e) No organ would have been able to check him: the unfair order would have stood, his friends' buildings would have stayed without fire exits, and residents would have been unsafe and treated unequally.
s: (a) Step 1 legislature; Step 4 executive
(b) Judiciary, examining whether an executive decision was right
(c) Executive overstepped: it must implement the law, not exempt some people
(d) The judiciary checked the executive and restored balance
(e) Without separation no one could check him; the unfair order would stand

questions.q: According to the chapter, at which three levels does the government function in India?
questions.a: Local, State and Central (Union)
o: Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha and Vidhan Sabha

questions.q: The Government of India's motto is Satyameva Jayate. What does it mean?
questions.a: Truth alone triumphs
o: Where there is dharma, there is victory
Dharma protects those who protect it

questions.q: After four days of heavy rain, a flood spreads over vast areas of a State. The State's rescue teams are already at work but cannot reach everyone. Going by the chapter, what may happen next?
questions.a: The Central Government may also come to help, sending relief supplies, the army and so on.
o: The Central Government may also help, sending relief and the army
The local authorities must manage alone, since floods begin locally
The State Government must hand the work over to the High Court
No more help can come, since the State is the highest level

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the chapter's comparison, if a bulb in your home is not lighting up, you first check the bulb, the switch and the fuse.
Reason (R): The chapter says the Electricity Board is the first place to go when a bulb at home does not light up.
questions.a: A is true but R is false. You go to the Electricity Board and file a complaint only if checking the bulb, switch and fuse and calling an electrician show that the problem is not within your home.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Name the three levels of government in India and state the level at which each one works, as shown in the chapter's pyramid (Fig. 10.4).
questions.a: Local government works at the town or village level; the State Government at the State level; the Central (Union) Government at the national level.
s: Names local, State and Central (Union) government
Matches them to the town or village, State and national levels

questions.q: True or False? 'The Central Government and the Union Government are two different levels of government in India.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. 'Central' and 'Union' are two names for the same government at the national level. India's three levels are local, State and Central (or Union) government.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: Central and Union name the same national-level government; the levels are local, State and Central

questions.q:
The tap in a family's kitchen stops running. They first check their own pipes and tap, then call a plumber, and when he finds the fault is outside the house they complain to the town's water office.
(a) How is this like the chapter's bulb comparison?
(b) What does the comparison teach about the three levels of government?
questions.a: (a) In both, a problem is dealt with at three levels: first by the family itself, then by a skilled helper (plumber or electrician), and finally by a body outside the home (water office or Electricity Board) only when the problem is not within the home. (b) Each level of government deals with different matters, and a problem goes to a higher level only when it is beyond the level below.
s: (a) Both pass a problem through three levels, going outside the home only when the fault is not within it
(b) Each level deals with different matters; a higher level comes in when the lower cannot deal with it

questions.q:
Answer from the chapter's flood example.
(i) If a flood in part of a district is not too severe, who may be able to deal with it?
(ii) If the flood involves several towns and many villages, what does the State Government do?
(iii) If it is a massive flood affecting vast areas, what may the Central Government send?
questions.a: (i) The local authorities. (ii) It steps in and sends rescue teams to help the affected people. (iii) Relief supplies, the army, etc.
s: (i) The local authorities
(ii) Steps in and sends rescue teams
(iii) Relief supplies and the army

questions.q:
Three problems arise in one year.
P: The only well in a village dries up, and 40 families lose drinking water.
Q: Swarms of insects damage crops in 9 districts of one State.
R: An earthquake damages towns in 4 States.
Using the chapter's idea of three levels, say which level of government would be expected to deal with each problem, or to step in, and state the rule you used to decide.
questions.a: P: the local government, as the problem is limited to one village. Q: the State Government, as it covers many districts of one State, too large for local authorities alone. R: the Central Government may also come to help, as the damage spreads over vast areas beyond one State. Rule: each level deals with different matters; the scale of the problem decides the level, and a higher level steps in when the problem is too large for the level below (as in the chapter's flood example).
s: P local and Q State, each linked to the area affected
R: the Central Government comes in because the damage spreads beyond one State
States the rule: the scale of the problem decides the level; higher levels step in when lower ones cannot cope

questions.q:
During a dry April, forest fires broke out in a hilly State. Day 1: a grass fire burnt 3 hectares near one village, and it was put out by evening by people from that village and its nearby town. Day 3: fires broke out near 26 villages spread over 4 districts of the State, and rescue teams were sent from the State capital. Day 6: fires were burning over vast forest areas in that State and in 2 neighbouring States, and soldiers and relief supplies arrived.
(a) Which level of government most likely handled the Day 1 fire?
(b) Which level sent the teams on Day 3, and why did it step in?
(c) Going by the chapter, which level most likely sent the soldiers and relief supplies on Day 6?
(d) On Day 3 an official wanted to ask for help from the highest level at once instead of waiting. Using the data and the chapter, give one point for and one against his view, and your judgement.
questions.a: (a) The local government, at the town or village level. (b) The State Government; the fires involved many villages over several districts, too large for local authorities alone, as when a flood involves several towns and many villages. (c) The Central Government, which may send relief supplies, the army, etc., when a disaster affects vast areas. (d) For: the fire spread from 3 hectares near one village to 26 villages in 2 days, so asking early might save time. Against: on Day 3 the fire was still within one State, which is the State Government's level, and each level deals with different matters. Judgement: the State should act first but warn the Central Government early, since the spread was fast; by Day 6 the scale did call for Central help.
s: (a) Local government
(b) State Government, because many villages over several districts were affected
(c) Central Government
(d) Gives one point each way from the data and a reasoned judgement

questions.q: In the chapter's table (Fig. 10.5), which pair correctly names the judiciary at the All India level and at the State level, in that order?
questions.a: Supreme Court of India; High Court
o: Supreme Court of India; High Court
High Court; Supreme Court of India
Supreme Court of India; Vidhan Sabha

questions.q: According to the chapter's table, what do the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha do?
questions.a: They formulate national laws.
o: Decide cases as the highest court

questions.q:
Match each body in Column A with its place in Column B, going by the chapter's table.
Column A:
1. Supreme Court of India
2. High Court
3. Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
4. Vidhan Sabha
Column B:
A. Legislature at the State level
B. Judiciary at the State level
C. Legislature at the national level
D. Judiciary at the All India level
Priya reads that a House 'discussed and passed a law for her State alone'. Going by the chapter's table, which body could this be?
questions.a: The Vidhan Sabha (State Assembly), the legislature at the State level. The Rajya Sabha, despite its name, is one of the two Houses that formulate national laws.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A few States in India have two Houses in their legislature.
Reason (R): At the national level, two Houses, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, formulate national laws.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. The table notes that most States have a single assembly and a few have two; the national legislature having two Houses does not explain why those few States have two.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: (a) What is a 'House', as the chapter's glossary defines it? (b) Name the House that formulates laws at the State level.
questions.a: (a) An assembly where laws are discussed or passed. (b) The State Assembly, or Vidhan Sabha.
s: (a) An assembly where laws are discussed or passed
(b) The State Assembly or Vidhan Sabha

questions.q:
Answer from the chapter's table (Fig. 10.5).
(i) To which organ of government does the Supreme Court of India belong?
(ii) Is the Rajya Sabha part of the legislature at the national level or at the State level?
(iii) Most States have a single assembly. What does the table note about the rest?
questions.a: (i) The judiciary. (ii) At the national level. (iii) A few States have two assemblies (Houses).
s: (i) The judiciary
(ii) The national level
(iii) A few States have two

questions.q: Compare the legislature at the national level with the legislature of a State, using the chapter's table. Write one point under each heading: (a) the name of the House or Houses; (b) the number of Houses; (c) whose laws they formulate; (d) why all of them are called Houses.
questions.a: (a) National: the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha; State: the State Assembly or Vidhan Sabha. (b) National: two Houses; State: most States have a single assembly, though a few have two. (c) National: laws for the whole nation (national laws); State: laws for that State. (d) Each is an assembly where laws are discussed or passed, which is what the chapter means by a House.
s: (a) Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha against State Assembly or Vidhan Sabha
(b) Two at the national level; one in most States, two in a few
(c) National laws against laws for the State
(d) Each is an assembly where laws are discussed or passed

questions.q:
Class 6 of a school in Indore went on a study tour to their State capital. In the morning they watched members of the State's law-making assembly discuss a new law on water for farms. After lunch they visited the highest court of the State, where a judge was hearing a dispute between two companies. Back at school, their teacher drew a chart of the legislature and the judiciary at the national and State levels and asked these questions.
(a) What does the chapter's table call the State assembly they watched in the morning?
(b) What is the name of the court they visited after lunch?
(c) Which court does the table show at the All India level?
(d) Why is the assembly they saw in the morning called a 'House', while the court is not?
questions.a: (a) The State Assembly, or Vidhan Sabha. (b) The High Court. (c) The Supreme Court of India. (d) A House is an assembly where laws are discussed or passed, which is what the members were doing; the court belongs to the judiciary, which decides cases such as disputes, not laws.
s: (a) State Assembly or Vidhan Sabha
(b) High Court
(c) Supreme Court of India
(d) A House discusses or passes laws; the court decides cases

questions.q:
Here are five newspaper headlines. For each, name the organ of government (legislature or judiciary) and the level (national/All India, or State) of the body named, using the chapter's table.
(a) 'Lok Sabha members debate a new national law'
(b) 'High Court hears a land dispute between two villages'
(c) 'Vidhan Sabha passes a law on irrigation canals'
(d) 'Supreme Court of India hears an appeal'
(e) 'Rajya Sabha discusses a national law on communications'
questions.a: (a) Legislature, national level. (b) Judiciary, State level. (c) Legislature, State level. (d) Judiciary, All India level. (e) Legislature, national level.
s: (a) Legislature, national
(b) Judiciary, State
(c) Legislature, State
(d) Judiciary, All India
(e) Legislature, national

questions.q: According to the chapter's table, who is the executive head of a State Government?
questions.a: The Chief Minister

questions.q: Farmers in a State need new canals to water their fields. Going by the chapter's table, on which government's list of functions does this fall, and who is the executive head of that government?
questions.a: The State Government (Irrigation is on its list), whose executive head is the Chief Minister.
o: The State Government; the Chief Minister
The Central Government; the Prime Minister

questions.q:
Match each line from a news report in Column A with the office it describes in Column B, going by the chapter's table.
Column A:
1. 'He is the Supreme Commander of the Indian Armed Forces.'
2. 'As the State's executive head, she announced a new public health plan.'
3. 'As the nominal head of the State, he normally does not interfere in the State government's affairs.'
4. 'As the executive head of the Central Government, he spoke about foreign affairs.'
Column B:
A. Prime Minister
B. Governor
C. President of India
D. Chief Minister

Consider the following statements about the chapter's table of executive functions.
I. Education appears on the lists of both the Central and the State Government.
II. Police, law and order is on the State Government's list.
III. The table says its lists of functions are not exhaustive.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: I, II and III: all three are correct.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam played an important role as President of India, impacting countless lives.
Reason (R): The President's position is nominal: the President is not the actual executive head and normally does not interfere in the affairs of the Central government.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. R explains why the President's powers are limited; Dr. Kalam's important role came despite this, through his connection with the people and the youth, his passion for education and innovation, and his humility.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: True or False? 'When a State government adapts a law made by the Central government and puts it into practice in the State, it is doing a job listed among the State Government's own functions in the chapter's table.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The State Government's list includes the adaptation and implementation of laws made by the Central government at the State level.
s: States the verdict: True
Reason: adaptation and implementation of Central laws at the State level is on the State list

questions.q:
(a) Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam served as the 11th President of India from 2002 to 2007. For how many years did he serve?
(b) Using the chapter's meaning of 'nominal', explain why the chapter still says he played an important role.
questions.a: (a) 2007 - 2002 = 5 years. (b) Nominal means 'in name only': the President is not the actual executive head. Yet Dr. Kalam stayed deeply connected to the people, especially the youth, through his passion for good education and innovation, and inspired millions, so he impacted countless lives even from a nominal post.
s: (a) 5 years
(b) Nominal means in name only, yet he influenced people through education, innovation and inspiring the youth

questions.a: (i) The State Government's list (police, law and order); executive head: the Chief Minister. (ii) The Central Government's list (atomic energy); executive head: the Prime Minister. (iii) The Central Government's list (foreign affairs); executive head: the Prime Minister.
s: (i) State list, police and law and order, Chief Minister
(ii) Central list, atomic energy, Prime Minister
(iii) Central list, foreign affairs, Prime Minister

questions.q:
In May, a State was hit by a 30-day heatwave. Its government hospitals treated 4,200 people for heatstroke, 1,800 of them in the first 10 days. The State's executive head announced 120 drinking-water kiosks and extra doctors for the hospitals. The State's nominal head visited a hospital and thanked the nurses. A student wrote in her school magazine: 'The nominal head did nothing useful. A post that is only a name is of no value.'
(a) Under which function on the State Government's list in the chapter's table does the hospitals' work fall?
(b) How many patients were treated in the last 20 days, and what was the average per day then? Compare it with the first 10 days.
(c) Name the office that announced the kiosks and the office that visited the hospital.
(d) Judge the student's view, using the chapter's meaning of 'nominal' and its example of Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.
questions.a: (a) Public health. (b) 4,200 - 1,800 = 2,400 patients in the last 20 days, an average of 2,400 / 20 = 120 a day, compared with 1,800 / 10 = 180 a day in the first 10 days. (c) The Chief Minister (executive head) announced the kiosks; the Governor (nominal head) visited the hospital. (d) The student is partly right: 'nominal' means in name only, so the Governor is not the actual executive head and normally does not interfere, which is why the Chief Minister ran the response. But the chapter's Kalam example shows that a nominal head can still play an important role by inspiring and connecting with people, so the post is not of no value.
s: (a) Public health
(b) 2,400 patients; 120 a day against 180 a day earlier
(c) Chief Minister announced; Governor visited
(d) Partly right: no executive role, yet the Kalam example shows real influence

questions.a: (a) Central: the President of India (also Supreme Commander of the Indian Armed Forces); State: the Governor. (b) Central: the Prime Minister; State: the Chief Minister. (c) Central, for example: defence, foreign affairs, atomic energy, communications, currency, inter-state commerce, formulation of national policies (any two); State, for example: police and law and order, public health, agriculture, irrigation, local government (any two). (d) Education. (e) The State Government adapts and implements laws made by the Central government at the State level, which is one of its listed functions; so the two executives work together.
s: (a) President against Governor as nominal heads
(b) Prime Minister against Chief Minister as executive heads
(c) Two Central-only and two State-only functions
(d) Education is on both lists
(e) The State adapts and implements Central laws at the State level

questions.q: In which of these situations is a decision taken through representative democracy, as the chapter describes it?
questions.a: People of an area elect an MLA, who discusses laws for them in the State Assembly.

All 30 members of a club raise hands to choose the place for their outing

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
I. In the word 'democracy', dēmos means 'rule' and kratos means 'people'.
II. Elected members are generally called MLAs at the State level and MPs at the national level.
III. When a class picks a picnic place by counting raised hands, it is using representative democracy, because the teacher organises the vote.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: II only. Statement I swaps the meanings: dēmos means 'people' and kratos means 'rule' or 'power'. Statement III is wrong: every student's opinion is counted, so it is direct democracy.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): India is a direct democracy, because its citizens choose who will govern them.
Reason (R): In principle, all Indian citizens above the age of 18 have the right to participate in elections.
questions.a: A is false but R is true. Citizens vote for representatives (MLAs and MPs) who decide on their behalf, so India is a representative democracy, not a direct one; the right to vote from above 18 is correct.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q: (a) What does the word 'democracy' literally mean? (b) Name the two Greek words it comes from and give the meaning of each.
questions.a: (a) 'Rule of the people'. (b) Dēmos, meaning 'people', and kratos, meaning 'rule' or 'power'.
s: (a) Rule of the people
(b) Dēmos = people; kratos = rule or power

questions.q:
Answer briefly from the chapter.
(i) What are the elected members of a State's assembly generally called?
(ii) What are the elected members at the national level called?
(iii) Above what age do Indian citizens, in principle, have the right to participate in elections?
questions.a: (i) Members of Legislative Assembly (MLAs). (ii) Members of Parliament (MPs). (iii) Above the age of 18.
s: (i) MLAs, Members of Legislative Assembly
(ii) MPs, Members of Parliament
(iii) Above 18

questions.q:
In a State Assembly, members elected from the hill districts want a new bridge built in the hills, while members from the plains want it built in the plains.
(i) What are these elected members generally called?
(ii) According to the chapter, how do such members try to settle their different opinions?
(iii) Why, in a democracy, is the decision left to these members rather than to every citizen of the State voting on it?
questions.a: (i) Members of Legislative Assembly (MLAs). (ii) They discuss the problem and its solutions in the assembly and, through dialogue and debate, try to convince each other. (iii) It is not practical for all the people of a State to decide directly, just as a whole class cannot go to the principal; so people elect representatives who decide on their behalf. This is representative democracy.
s: (i) MLAs
(ii) Through discussion, dialogue and debate, trying to convince each other
(iii) Not everyone can decide directly, so elected representatives decide on the people's behalf

questions.q: The chapter compares a class sending its class representative to the principal with the way India is governed. Explain this comparison in four steps: (a) why the whole class does not go to the principal; (b) who, at the State and national levels, are like the class that chooses; (c) who, at each level, are like the class representative; (d) what these representatives do once they are elected.
questions.a: (a) It would not be practical for the entire class to go; one elected or selected representative is enough. (b) The people (citizens), who vote in elections. (c) The elected members of the assemblies: MLAs at the State level and MPs at the national level. (d) They discuss laws, problems and solutions in the assemblies and, through dialogue and debate, try to convince each other when there are different opinions.
s: (a) It is not practical for everyone to go; one representative is enough
(b) The citizens who vote
(c) MLAs at the State level, MPs at the national level
(d) They discuss laws, problems and solutions through dialogue and debate

questions.q:
The 210 students of Class 6 in a Bhopal school took two decisions this month. Decision 1: to choose the theme of Sports Day, all 210 students met in the hall and raised hands; 128 voted for 'Olympics' and the rest for 'Asian Games'. Decision 2: each of the 6 sections elected one student, and these 6 students met the principal to ask for a water cooler on their floor. Next month they must decide whether lunch break should move from 11:30 am to 12 noon.
(a) How many students voted for 'Asian Games', and by how many votes did 'Olympics' win?
(b) Which kind of democracy was Decision 1? Give a reason.
(c) Which kind was Decision 2, and who play a similar role for the people at the State level?
(d) Which way should they use for the lunch-break decision? Give one advantage of each way and your choice.
questions.a: (a) 210 - 128 = 82 voted for 'Asian Games'; 'Olympics' won by 128 - 82 = 46 votes. (b) Direct democracy: every student's own opinion was counted towards the decision. (c) Representative democracy; MLAs, elected by the people, play a similar role at the State level. (d) Direct voting counts every student's opinion, and the lunch break affects all 210 and they can all meet in the hall; representatives are quicker and can discuss the pros and cons with the principal. A reasonable choice is direct voting, since everyone is affected and a show of hands is practical for 210 students (choosing representatives is also acceptable if justified).
s: (a) 82 votes; won by 46
(b) Direct democracy, as every student's opinion was counted
(c) Representative democracy; MLAs
(d) One advantage of each way and a justified choice

questions.q:
A township in Lucknow has 2,400 residents, of whom 1,500 are above 18. They must decide how to use an empty plot: a playground or a small library. Plan A: the residents' committee of 9 members, elected by the residents, decides after a debate. Plan B: every resident above 18 votes. In a trial vote under Plan B, 900 residents voted, and 495 of them chose the playground.
(a) What percentage of the residents above 18 took part in the trial vote?
(b) What percentage of those who voted chose the playground?
(c) Which plan is direct democracy and which is representative democracy?
(d) Which plan fits the chapter's idea of grassroots democracy better? Weigh the trial vote's data in your answer.
questions.a: (a) 900 / 1,500 x 100 = 60%. (b) 495 / 900 x 100 = 55%. (c) Plan B is direct democracy (each voter's own opinion counts); Plan A is representative democracy (elected members decide on the residents' behalf). (d) Plan B fits grassroots democracy better, since grassroots democracy enables and encourages ordinary citizens to have a say in decisions that affect them. But the data show its limits: 40% of adults did not vote, and the playground won only 55% of the votes cast (495 of 1,500 adults, about one-third). A good judgement keeps the vote but encourages more residents to take part, or lets the committee debate the result.
s: (c) Plan B direct, Plan A representative
(d) Plan B fits grassroots democracy, weighed against the 40% who did not vote

questions.q: 'Democracy literally means the rule of the people, yet in India the people do not all rule directly.' Justify this statement using the chapter. Your answer should cover: (a) the meaning of the word; (b) why all people cannot rule; (c) how Indians choose who decides for them; (d) how those chosen reach decisions; (e) how ordinary citizens can still have a say.
questions.a: (a) 'Democracy' comes from dēmos (people) and kratos (rule or power), so it means rule of the people. (b) It is not possible for all people to actually rule, just as it is not practical for a whole class to go to the principal. (c) Through elections, citizens above 18 vote for representatives: MLAs at the State level and MPs at the national level. India, with some 970 million voters in 2024, is the world's largest democracy and a representative democracy. (d) The representatives discuss laws, problems and solutions in the assemblies and, through dialogue and debate, try to convince each other. (e) Grassroots democracy enables and encourages ordinary citizens, the base of the pyramid, to have a say in decisions that affect them, so the people still rule through their choices and participation.
s: (a) Meaning: rule of the people (dēmos, kratos)
(b) Not all can rule directly; it is not practical
(c) Citizens above 18 elect MLAs and MPs; India is a representative democracy
(d) Representatives decide through dialogue and debate in assemblies
(e) Grassroots democracy gives ordinary citizens a say
